header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 16:00 PT
Duration: 56 minutes
Attendees: Evan Martinez (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Michael Chen (Northshore VP Eng), Sara Ortiz (Head of ML), Tom Reynolds (Cloud Infra), Aisha Malik (Security)
Summary: Discovery focused on Dedicated capacity for low-latency trading/analysis workloads, data isolation and VPC requirements, burst/overcommit strategy, and scaling expectations. Customer needs SOC2/KMS assurances and a benchmark plan.
Topics: Dedicated capacity sizing, isolation (VPC & on-prem), burst policies & autoscaling, latency vs cost tradeoffs, security & compliance, next steps
transcript:
[00:00] Evan Martinez: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Evan from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account. we've got Priya and Liam from the engineering side, and on the Northshore side hi michael sarah tom thanks for taking the time
[00:12] Michael Chen: Yep thanks Evan, appreciate it. real quick agenda, we're trying to understand dedicated capacity, what committed GPUs look like, isolation needs, and what bursting or overflow would be, plus security questions.
[00:22] Priya Desai: Cool, i'll kick off with a quick overview of Dedicated — it's reserved GPU pools for customers that need predictable throughput and stronger isolation. You get a dedicated set of nodes, private network peering or VPC, and optional on-prem packaging if needed. Latency SLOs are more predictable because you're not noisy-neighboring.
[00:37] Sara Ortiz: Question: we run a lot of short generation tasks, 100–300 tokens, but very spiky at market open. We need 95th and 99th percentile latency guarantees. How do you size for bursts without wasting on commit?
[00:52] Liam O'Connor: Good question. Typical pattern is base reserved capacity sized to cover steady-state QPS and then a burst pool that can be either shared across tenants in your org or on-demand that Redwood can burst into depending on commit level. We also do autoscaling policies — you can set threshold-based scale-ups, and we support burst credits to absorb short spikes.
[01:10] Tom Reynolds: Are those bursts running on the same hardware or are they public clouds? we need isolation for sensitive prompts.
[01:18] Priya Desai: You can configure burst to use dedicated warm nodes within your Dedicated fleet or to spill over to hosted capacity. For highly-sensitive data we strongly recommend keeping bursts within your Dedicated pool or Private deployment. spilling to hosted means you'd need to accept that data path.
[01:33] Aisha Malik: Can you walk through encryption and KMS? we use customer-managed keys and require envelope encryption for logs and model inputs.
[01:40] Priya Desai: Absolutely. In Dedicated we integrate with customer KMS (AWS KMS / GCP KMS / Azure Key Vault). We support CMKs for model payload encryption at rest and we can enable in-transit TLS with mutual auth for private peering. Audit logs can be exported to your SIEM and are retained per your contract. On Private we can do HSM integrations for highest assurance.
[02:01] Michael Chen: for throughput, our baseline is 400 qps steady, with 4,000 qps spikes for 30–60s at market open. Tail latency target is p99 < 250ms for single-turn text generation of small prompts. cost is obviously a factor. how would you approach sizing?
[02:20] Liam O'Connor: baseline 400 qps — first step is quantifying tokens per request and average sequence length. with short 100–300 tokens at say 40 tokens per second per GPU (varies by model), we would estimate N GPUs for steady-state and then add burst capacity for headroom. But because you have short spikes it's often cost-efficient to use warm standby capacity + burst credits vs full commit. we can run a benchmark with your payloads to produce a sizing doc.
[02:42] Sara Ortiz: are you supporting quantized models? we want to reduce GPU memory and cost.
[02:48] Priya Desai: Yes — we support int8/4 quantization paths and recommend specific model variants. The runtime will choose kernels and quant profiles based on seq length and hardware, that helps reduce memory so a single GPU serves more concurrent requests.
[02:59] Michael Chen: what about model variants / fallback — if our main model is busy do you have automatic fallback to smaller models to keep latency?
[03:06] Priya Desai: We have smart routing and policy-based fallbacks. You can configure cost vs latency policies: prefer primary model, then fallback to a quantized variant or a smaller architecture. We also support graceful degradation, like returning cached prefixes for repeated prompts.
[03:22] Tom Reynolds: on networking, we need VPC peering and private control plane. can you do all control plane traffic over our private network?
[03:29] Liam O'Connor: For Dedicated we offer VPC peering + private endpoints. The control plane can be configured to use a private control plane for Private deployments; for Hosted Dedicated there's still a management plane but data plane can be fully private. we'll detail the options in the security doc.
[03:45] Aisha Malik: SOC2 and pen-test reports — do you have SOC2 Type II? we need evidence for our auditors.
[03:50] Priya Desai: Redwood has SOC2 Type II attestation; we can share SOC2 report along with our penetration testing summary and our standard security questionnaire. For Private we can offer additional compliance artifacts.
[04:02] Michael Chen: from a procurement standpoint, how are billing and reserved capacity contracts structured? monthly commit? annual? discounts?
[04:08] Evan Martinez: We offer monthly and annual committed tiers. Pricing varies by GPU class, commit level, and add-ons like increased retention, extended observability. Typically bigger commits get steeper discounts and higher SLA credits. We'll send a pricing matrix.
[04:22] Sara Ortiz: do you have per-route dashboards and token-level cost visibility? we want to see which models/routes cost the most by feature.
[04:28] Priya Desai: Yep, Redwood Console gives per-route/model dashboards, token-level cost breakdowns, tracing hooks, and error analysis. You can instrument SDK calls to tag routes and get cost slices.
[04:40] Michael Chen: we have in-house inference for some models, but it's brittle and hard to operate. what's the onboarding path? POC? benchmark?
[04:47] Liam O'Connor: Common approach: pilot with Dedicated trial — we allocate a small reserved pool, run benchmarks with your sample prompts, test burst behavior during simulated spikes, and validate SLOs. After benchmark we iterate on quant profiles and batching to optimize unit cost.
[05:03] Tom Reynolds: about autoscaling — how fast can you scale up under load? we couldn't afford slow spin-up during market open.
[05:09] Priya Desai: For Dedicated, warm standby nodes can be kept in a ready state so scaling is effectively instant. Cold scaling (creating new instances) takes longer, so for market open bursts we recommend warm standby capacity or reserved burst credits. Policies can be set to pre-scale based on cron triggers (e.g., market open times).
[05:26] Sara Ortiz: any support for container-based on-prem install? we are in a bank regulated environment and might need to host on-prem.
[05:33] Priya Desai: Yes we have a Private on-prem package that includes the control plane software you run in your VPC or air-gapped environment. It includes the runtime, observability stack integrations, and the orchestration components. We have a separate enterprise licensing and support plan for that.
[05:46] Michael Chen: latency vs cost — can you show examples of tradeoffs? how much do we save by moving to quantized models and batching?
[05:54] Liam O'Connor: Rough ballpark: quantization can reduce GPU footprint 2–4x depending on model, batching improves throughput but increases per-request latency slightly; for short 100-token requests batching is modest benefit unless you have extremely high concurrency. We'll run your payloads to give concrete numbers.
[06:10] Aisha Malik: audit logs and data retention — we need tamper-evident logs and a retention policy controlled by us.
[06:16] Priya Desai: Audit logs can be exported to your SIEM and we can enable WORM-style retention in your storage if required. For Dedicated we can set retention in the contract, and for Private you control retention entirely.
[06:29] Michael Chen: any known limitations around model sizes, KV cache, or sequence lengths that would affect us? we do rolling 4k token contexts for some strategies.
[06:38] Priya Desai: We support long contexts; runtime picks kernels and handles KV cache efficiently. For very long contexts we may recommend larger GPU classes or model sharding. KV cache persistence and prefix caching can help for repeated context. We'll map out recommendations in the sizing doc.
[06:54] Sara Ortiz: do you support function-calling / structured outputs? our downstream systems expect JSON with strict schemas.
[07:00] Priya Desai: Yes we support structured outputs and function-calling style. We also have deterministic sampling modes and eval tools to validate schema adherence.
[07:10] Michael Chen: quick note — latency target is p99 < 250ms; if you can hit that on Dedicated with some burst plan we can move forward to POC.
[07:19] Evan Martinez: understoood. we'll prioritize that in the benchmark.
[07:23] Tom Reynolds: about network egress and data residency — we have customers in EMEA and need data to stay in-region.
[07:30] Priya Desai: We have region-aware deployments. For Dedicated we can pin capacity in specific regions and ensure data plane stays in-region. For Private you control physical location.
[07:40] Sara Ortiz: what's the usual timeline from pilot to production?
[07:44] Liam O'Connor: For a focused pilot with benchmarks it's typically 4–8 weeks: setup, benchmark, tune quantization & batching, validate SLOs, and then plan cutover. Onboarding can be sped up with more resources and pre-filled configs.
[07:58] Aisha Malik: regarding pen tests, do you allow our third-party auditors to do an assessment on Dedicated?
[08:04] Priya Desai: We have a process for that — for Dedicated we can provide scoped testing windows and a controls checklist. For Hosted there are stricter constraints; for Private you can run your full assessment.
[08:16] Michael Chen: what about SLAs and credits, what's typical?
[08:19] Evan Martinez: SLA targets vary by commit level. For Dedicated enterprise tiers we offer uptime SLA and latency SLOs with credits for breaches. We'll include example SLA language in the docs.
[08:30] (short pause)
[08:33] Michael Chen: ok let's talk numbers — what's the minimum commit you'd recommend for our 400 qps baseline?
[08:38] Liam O'Connor: Without exact tokens per request it's rough, but I would recommend a base commit for say 25–35% above baseline for steady state to account for variability, plus a burst pool sized to hit your 4,000 qps for the 30–60s spikes. Many customers do base commit for 500–600 qps and then a reserved burst or burst credits. We'll put numbers after we run the benchmark.
[08:58] Sara Ortiz: are there case studies with financial clients?
[09:01] Priya Desai: We have references and case studies; we can share anonymized performance benchmarks from other financial customers and a reference contact.
[09:10] Tom Reynolds: any gotchas with rate limiting and backpressure?
[09:14] Liam O'Connor: We support client-side and server-side rate limiting, token-based quotas, and can set graceful backpressure and queueing policies. For low-latency uses we prefer pre-scaling.
[09:26] Michael Chen: ok actions agreed, send pricing and benchmark plan, we'll deliver sample payloads and traces.
[09:31] Evan Martinez: captured. quick recap?
[09:34] Evan Martinez: Recap — Redwood to send pricing matrix, benchmark harness & runbook, security docs (SOC2 + pen test summaries), and proposed sizing for base + burst. Northshore to share payloads, traffic traces, and security questionnaire answers. Schedule security deep-dive with Aisha.
[09:52] Sara Ortiz: yep sounds good. thanks everyone.
[09:55] Michael Chen: thanks, bye.
